{"id": "20:21/q05", "question": "Why did Moses fear the serpent?", "turns_on": "The explanations locate the object of fear in the snake's danger, God's power, Adam's precedent, or loss of the staff's uses.", "positions": [{"id": "20:21/q05/p1", "position": "He reacted with ordinary human fear to a terrifying and unfamiliar serpent.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says extreme panic can overwhelm knowledge; al-Iṣlāḥī notes that Moses' staff for killing a snake had itself become one. Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Qurṭubī, al-Biqāʿī, Bursevī and al-Ālūsī call such fear natural; al-Ālūsī says it does not lessen prophetic rank. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ cites 28:31 for flight."}, {"id": "20:21/q05/p2", "position": "He feared being overwhelmed by divine might, rather than ordinary creaturely danger.", "reasons": "Junayd distinguishes fear of divine power from instinctive fear; al-Wāsiṭī sees on the staff a sign of divine displeasure and punishment, making hidden divine power unsettling. Al-Ālūsī reports a comparison: Moses faced a mysterious act from God, while Abraham faced a known fire from an enemy."}, {"id": "20:21/q05/p3", "position": "He feared because a serpent had figured in Adam's misfortune or expulsion.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and al-Ālūsī transmit this explanation without adopting it."}, {"id": "20:21/q05/p4", "position": "He feared losing the uses and benefits of his staff.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī rejects this as misjudging Moses' spiritual standing."}]}
{"id": "20:21/q06", "question": "What shows that Moses was afraid, and what does that fear imply?", "turns_on": "The notes distinguish evidence of fear, its value as a sign of sincerity, and its compatibility with prophetic courage.", "positions": [{"id": "20:21/q06/p1", "position": "His flight shows actual fear; the prohibition alone would not establish it.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī compares 'do not fear' with 33:1's 'do not obey the disbelievers': a prohibition does not prove the forbidden action. He cites Moses' flight in 27:10 and contrasts Muhammad's freedom from worldly attachment. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ cites 28:31; Study Quran points to 27:10 and 28:31."}, {"id": "20:21/q06/p2", "position": "His fear attests truthful prophethood.", "reasons": "Abū al-Qāsim al-Anṣārī argues that a magician knows a display is illusion and therefore would not fear it."}, {"id": "20:21/q06/p3", "position": "Ordinary prophetic fear differs from blameworthy inner agitation.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ defines khawf as taking precautions against harm and khashya as disturbance of the heart; prophets can experience the first but not cowardly khashya, citing 33:39."}]}
{"id": "20:21/q07", "question": "When and why did Moses cease fearing?", "turns_on": "The reports attach reassurance to the command, to the promised restoration, or place residual fear after both.", "positions": [{"id": "20:21/q07/p1", "position": "God's promise to restore the serpent to a staff reassured him.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports that some commentators connect the fear's end to the promise, citing 27:10–11. Al-Ālūsī says the promise explains both obedience and fearlessness."}, {"id": "20:21/q07/p2", "position": "God's command not to fear brought tranquility and ended his fear.", "reasons": "Study Quran attributes this to other commentators, citing 27:10–11; al-Rāzī reports a view that the command removed fear sufficiently for Moses to grasp the jaws. Bursevī says God removed the initial fear."}, {"id": "20:21/q07/p3", "position": "He remained frightened even while taking it.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī rejects this report as unlikely after accumulated signs and God's restoration promise."}]}
{"id": "20:21/q08", "question": "What is the force of 'do not fear' beside the command to take it?", "turns_on": "Whether 'do not fear' is an independent end or chiefly reassurance attached to taking the serpent.", "positions": [{"id": "20:21/q08/p1", "position": "Fearlessness is itself intended, in addition to enabling Moses to take the serpent.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī bases this on coordination of the prohibition with the positive command."}, {"id": "20:21/q08/p2", "position": "The prohibition reassures Moses that the serpent will become his staff again.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī and Asad couple reassurance with restoration; al-Ālūsī says the promise is why he should take it without fear."}]}
{"id": "20:21/q09", "question": "Why was Moses shown and told to take this sign before facing Pharaoh?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize either preparation for Pharaoh or further proof through the reversal.", "positions": [{"id": "20:21/q09/p1", "position": "The prior experience trained him not to panic when the staff changed before Pharaoh.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī says the miracle prepared Moses and that this verse implies fear which al-Qaṣaṣ states; the exegetes in al-Baghawī call it a sign beyond human ability. Al-Qurṭubī, al-Nasafī, al-Biqāʿī, Bursevī and Study Quran make the same preparatory connection. Al-Ālūsī reports it as a proposed wisdom but calls the further claim that the promise itself is a new reassuring sign unclear."}, {"id": "20:21/q09/p2", "position": "Taking the live serpent safely and seeing it become wood added miracles to the first transformation.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says the two further signs strengthened the proof; al-Biqāʿī says the sign confirmed that the speaker was the Lord with the most beautiful names."}]}
{"id": "20:21/q10", "question": "What does sīrah mean here and how did that sense arise?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:21/q10/p1", "position": "It means a way, manner, form, or condition, extended from movement or travel.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, al-Zajjāj, al-Jishumī, al-Nasafī, Bursevī, al-Ālūsī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ connect the word to a mode of going; al-Zajjāj notes its use for resemblance though ṭarīqa and sīra often describe acts. Al-Kashshāf, cited by al-Rāzī, compares rukba from riding; al-Samīn compares the same form and cites Khālid al-Hudhalī's poetry. Abū Ḥayyān also cites a poem; al-Ālūsī notes a line for 'way' or school. Ibn ʿAbbās glosses condition, Mujāhid appearance, Abū ʿUbayda original creation."}]}
{"id": "20:21/q11", "question": "What does God promise by 'We shall restore it to its former sīrah'?", "turns_on": "The ordinary explanation identifies a literal staff; al-Qāshānī reads the first state as a condition of the soul.", "positions": [{"id": "20:21/q11/p1", "position": "The serpent will return to the staff's original form, state, and familiar uses.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, Qatāda, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jurayj, Wahb, ʿAṭāʾ and al-Suddī give forms of this gloss. Al-Ṭabarī invokes Arabic usage for resuming a former state; al-Jishumī defines iʿāda as a second return to an original state. Al-Mubarrad says it will be as before; al-Wāḥidī and al-Bayḍāwī include its former behavior; al-Biqāʿī says God's promise cannot fail. Abū ʿUbayda calls it original creation. Abū Zayd notes the construction can use ilā."}, {"id": "20:21/q11/p2", "position": "In an inward reading, its first condition is lifeless, vegetative capacity without awareness or impulse.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī relates the staff to Moses' training under Shuʿayb and says Shuʿayb gave it to him."}]}
{"id": "20:21/q12", "question": "How is the accusative sīratahā construed?", "turns_on": "The alternatives differ over omitted prepositions, direct transitivity, adverbial force, apposition, or an implied verb; Abū Ḥayyān disputes the adverbial analysis.", "positions": [{"id": "20:21/q12/p1", "position": "An omitted preposition, especially ilā, licenses the accusative.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān, Abū Isḥāq and others restore ilā; ʿAlī compares 7:155, 'Moses chose his people.' Al-Ḥawfī says ilā or li; Ibn Mālik adopts and Ibn Hishām approves this analysis according to al-Ālūsī. Al-Burhān instead supplies ʿalā. Al-Bayḍāwī also allows derivation from causative ʿāda."}, {"id": "20:21/q12/p2", "position": "The verb directly governs sīratahā as a second object.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī allows direct governance; al-Ḥawfī and al-Zamakhsharī analyze ʿāda as 'return to.' Al-Samīn cites Zuhayr's line; al-Ālūsī also cites al-Aṣmaʿī and lexicographers for transitive ʿāda, while his report of the Zuhayr line glosses ʿādaka as 'turned you away.'"}, {"id": "20:21/q12/p3", "position": "It is an adverbial accusative, 'in its former manner.'", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Nasafī allow this. Abū Ḥayyān objects that a specific adverb needs fī and its omission is rare or poetic; al-Ālūsī cites Maghribī grammarians who treat such derived nouns as an indefinite adverbial type, making this regular."}, {"id": "20:21/q12/p4", "position": "It is an apposition of inclusion replacing the object pronoun and specifying its former quality.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥawfī and Abū al-Baqāʾ give the replacement analysis; al-Samīn describes it as apposition of inclusion."}, {"id": "20:21/q12/p5", "position": "The restoration verb is complete, and sīratahā belongs to an understood verb or clause describing its former movement.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī estimates tasīru and the staff's former uses; Abū Ḥayyān prefers this third parse. Al-Samīn supplies yasīru as a circumstantial clause. Al-Zamakhsharī, cited by al-Ālūsī, treats it as an absolute object, recalling Moses' leaning on the staff and using it for his flock. Al-Ālūsī likes its meaning but says it departs from the apparent construction."}, {"id": "20:21/q12/p6", "position": "Sīratahā is a verbal noun corresponding to an implied sense 'make it proceed.'", "reasons": "ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān says sanʿīduhā carries the sense sanusayyiruhā."}]}
{"id": "20:21/q13", "question": "What did the serpent look and act like when Moses fled?", "turns_on": "Reports vary in visual details and in whether the transformed creature posed real danger.", "positions": [{"id": "20:21/q13/p1", "position": "It was a terrifying, powerful serpent that swallowed or crushed objects and made Moses flee.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās says it swallowed a tree and rock, and M

oses heard the rock; Wahb mentions fangs. Al-Ṭabrisī reports a camel-sized creature crossing rock, uprooting a tree, fiery eyes and a meteor-haired neck, with Moses stopping from shame before God. Al-Bayḍāwī says it moved fast and swallowed stones and trees. Bursevī describes blazing eyes, grinding fangs, and jaws forty or eighty cubits apart."}, {"id": "20:21/q13/p2", "position": "The serpent was male.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās reports the sex in al-Ālūsī; Bursevī also calls it male."}, {"id": "20:21/q13/p3", "position": "It was a prophetic sign rather than a genuinely dangerous snake.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī records this explanation as a reason Moses could take it calmly."}]}
{"id": "20:21/q14", "question": "How do the descriptions jān, ḥayya, and great serpent fit together?", "turns_on": "Whether the verses describe successive stages or simultaneous size and movement.", "positions": [{"id": "20:21/q14/p1", "position": "Jān describes its first stage and great serpent its final stage; ḥayya covers snakes of any size or sex.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī reconciles the descriptions in 7:107 and 27:10 by sequence and broad usage."}, {"id": "20:21/q14/p2", "position": "It had a great serpent's body but a jān's speed and light movement.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī reports al-Zajjāj's reconciliation of 7:107 and 27:10."}]}
{"id": "20:21/q15", "question": "What is reported about the staff's origin?", "turns_on": "The reports assign the staff's provenance to Paradise, an angelic delivery, or Shuʿayb's gift.", "positions": [{"id": "20:21/q15/p1", "position": "It came from Paradise as Adam's staff and fell to Moses when Shuʿayb sent him to choose one.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports this account and separately reports Paradise myrtle as the wood; these details may belong to the same Paradise provenance."}, {"id": "20:21/q15/p2", "position": "An angel brought the staff to Moses.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī gives both an unnamed angel and Gabriel as variants of the bearer."}, {"id": "20:21/q15/p3", "position": "Shuʿayb gave Moses the staff.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī mentions this report in his inward account of Moses' training."}]}
{"id": "20:21/q16", "question": "What further abilities are reported for the staff?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:21/q16/p1", "position": "It later walked, spoke, carried loads, gave light, served as a bucket, and bore fruit.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī transmits these abilities as an unattributed report."}]}
{"id": "20:21/q17", "question": "Can the staff really change into a serpent and back?", "turns_on": "Whether essences themselves can change and, if so, how divine creation accounts for changed properties.", "positions": [{"id": "20:21/q17/p1", "position": "Yes; divine creative command can change a thing's reality.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī takes the verse as evidence and rejects the denial of transformation."}, {"id": "20:21/q17/p2", "position": "No; essences cannot change into other essences, so such change is impossible.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this denial and argues against it."}, {"id": "20:21/q17/p3", "position": "Transformation can be described as God creating gold in copper's place.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this explanatory model by analogy; it avoids simultaneous contrary identities."}, {"id": "20:21/q17/p4", "position": "Transformation can be described as removing copper's property and creating gold's property in atoms receptive to both.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī attributes this model to some theologians and favors it; copper and gold existing at once in the same thing is the impossible case."}]}
{"id": "20:21/q18", "question": "What inward meaning is given to taking the staff without fear?", "turns_on": "The inward readers identify the serpent with anger, feared causes, the lower soul, apparent reality, or changing spiritual states.", "positions": [{"id": "20:21/q18/p1", "position": "Moses regains intellectual control over an anger that now moves by God's command.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says the anger no longer hides beneath the heart's light, so Moses need not fear its domination or changes in spiritual state."}, {"id": "20:21/q18/p2", "position": "Only God causes harm and benefit, so fear and hope should be directed to Him alone.", "reasons": "The Najmī inward reading contrasts Moses' former belief in the staff's benefits with fear of its harm; Bursevī quotes the Mathnawī that one who fears God and has piety need fear no creature."}, {"id": "20:21/q18/p3", "position": "The serpent images the unrefined lower soul, which must be conquered and restored to its primordial disposition.", "reasons": "Study Quran attributes this to philosophers and mystics; Mullā Ṣadrā urges purification and an intellectual life oriented toward the Return and Final Abode."}, {"id": "20:21/q18/p4", "position": "The change alludes to appearances versus reality and insight granted to chosen servants.", "reasons": "Asad links it to Moses' encounter with the unnamed sage in 18:66–82 and wording in 27:10 and 28:31."}, {"id": "20:21/q18/p5", "position": "Changing states show God stabilizing servants as He gathers and separates them.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī reads the staff's sequence of changes as a pattern of spiritual states."}]}
{"id": "20:21/q19", "question": "What does the serpent image teach about the forms of deeds and traits?", "turns_on": "The accompanying analogies concern either the afterlife form of traits or the practical transformation of the knower.", "positions": [{"id": "20:21/q19/p1", "position": "Inner traits and deeds can appear in fitting perceptible forms in the next life.", "reasons": "Bursevī cites a hadith in which unpaid zakat appears as a serpent and 6:108 for deeds being shown; he says love of wealth in the commanding soul appears as a harmful snake, whereas purified love of spending in God's way takes a beautiful form. He extends the analogy to other traits."}, {"id": "20:21/q19/p2", "position": "Knowledge must turn into action and transform the person.", "reasons": "Bursevī quotes a Persian couplet about leaving base existence for love's alchemy and Jāmī's copper-to-gold image: knowledge without action is poison and achieves nothing."}]}
{"id": "20:21/q20", "question": "How do the prophets' experiences of fear compare?", "turns_on": "The comparisons appeal either to differing spiritual firmness or to the nature and source of what each prophet encountered.", "positions": [{"id": "20:21/q20/p1", "position": "Abraham's greater firmness explains why he did not fear the fire as Moses initially feared the staff.", "reasons": "Bursevī says God then removed Moses' fear so he reached Abraham's firmness."}, {"id": "20:21/q20/p2", "position": "Moses faced an unknown act from God, whereas Abraham knew the nature of fire brought by God's enemy.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this explanation of their different responses."}, {"id": "20:21/q20/p3", "position": "The Prophet likewise initially feared Gabriel, then became ready to see his true form.", "reasons": "Bursevī cites the Miʿrāj and 53:13–14 as a parallel progression."}]}
{"id": "20:21/q21", "question": "What distinguishes tafsīr and taʾwīl in handling a verse?", "turns_on": "The distinction turns on transmitted knowledge of revelation circumstances versus constrained inference from wording and context.", "positions": [{"id": "20:21/q21/p1", "position": "Tafsīr uncovers a verse's meaning and its transmitted revelation circumstances.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī derives it from uncovering, illustrated by driving a horse or camel until its hair or covering wears away; an unnamed Hudhalī verse supports the camel usage, though its wording is omitted. Scholars define tafsīr as knowledge of revelation, story, and causes; they restrict claims about revelation circumstances to transmitted reports."}, {"id": "20:21/q21/p2", "position": "Taʾwīl turns wording toward a possible contextual meaning, judged by Qurʾan and Sunna.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī links the word to return and the phrase awwaltuhu, 'I redirected it'; al-Naḍr instead derives it from iyāla, governance, because the interpreter manages speech. Scholars allow inference supported by wording and use Qurʾan and Sunna as its measure. Al-Thaʿlabī says the tafʿīl pattern of both terms implies repeated work through sūras and verses."}]}
{"id": "20:21/q22", "question": "What makes an elaborate expression rhetorically effective?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:21/q22/p1", "position": "Careful composition can make a normally heavy construction delicate and witty when it avoids affectation.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī cites Ibn al-Muʿtazz, al-Khālidī, Abū Tammām and al-Mutanabbī; even the familiar metaphor of being bound by kindness gains beauty through its path of phrasing."}]}
{"id": "20:26/q01", "question": "What does 'make easy' mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:26/q01/p1", "position": "Make easy rather than difficult.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī explicitly defines taysīr by its opposite, making difficult."}]}

{"id": "20:26/q03", "question": "What does 'for me' add to the request?", "turns_on": "Whether lī primarily intensifies the expression, connects the benefit to Moses, or specifies how ease affects him.", "positions": [{"id": "20:26/q03/p1", "position": "It leaves the object initially implicit and then specifies 'my affair,' emphasizing the plea.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī says the general request followed by particulars is stronger than a direct request; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī say the initial lī delays specification, and al-Ālūsī not

Al-Nasafī treats the repetition of general and particular as reinforcement; al-Suyūṭī explains that clarification after suspense strengthens understanding and pleasure."}, {"id": "20:26/q03/p2", "position": "It marks a stronger personal connection between Moses and the request.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this view and compares 21:1; he says it is compatible with the emphasis through delayed specification."}, {"id": "20:26/q03/p3", "position": "It shows that the benefit of the eased task returns to Moses.", "reasons": "Al-Intiṣāf says God is unaffected by the opening of Moses's chest; al-Ālūsī applies the same reasoning to easing his affair."}, {"id": "20:26/q03/p4", "position": "It specifies ease for Moses personally while the mission retains its demands.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says lī specifies the task entrusted to Moses; Moses seeks personal ease, not a reduced or compromised mission."}]}
{"id": "20:26/q04", "question": "How is the first-person yāʾ in 'for me' read?", "turns_on": "The transmitted treatment of the first-person yāʾ by each reader.", "positions": [{"id": "20:26/q04/p1", "position": "It is opened, yielding liya before amrī.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid assigns opening here to Nāfiʿ and Abū ʿAmr while noting their exceptions elsewhere; Ibn al-Jazarī adds Abū Jaʿfar and calls the group the two Medinese readers and Abū ʿAmr. Qiraat-ER states that the open vowel before amrī is a canonical variant. The lists also name other first-person yāʾs and their differing treatment."}, {"id": "20:26/q04/p2", "position": "It is kept still, yielding lī before amrī.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid assigns sukūn here to Ibn Kathīr, and to Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, Ibn ʿĀmir, and ʿĀṣim through Abū Bakr; their other listed first-person yāʾs vary or are all still respectively. Qiraat-ER says this too is canonical."}]}
{"id": "20:26/q05", "question": "How should a recited yāʾ be articulated?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:26/q05/p1", "position": "Give each yāʾ its proper light articulation and length, learned through oral practice.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī says a moving yāʾ should be gentle without becoming hamza, a madd yāʾ should receive its due length especially before another moving yāʾ, and a doubled yāʾ should remain one clear articulation without exaggerated stretching or constriction. Repetition with a teacher fixes the sound."}]}
{"id": "20:26/q06", "question": "What is Moses asking God to ease in 'my affair'?", "turns_on": "The scope of 'my affair' and whether ease names the mission's means, its outcome, all prophetic duties, or Moses's own capacity.", "positions": [{"id": "20:26/q06/p1", "position": "His commissioned mission of conveying God's message to Pharaoh and calling him to truth.", "reasons": "Muqātil contrasts ease with difficulty; Ibn ʿAbbās calls it the task for which Moses was sent. Al-Ṭabrisī mentions entering a tyrant's presence; al-Bayḍāwī, al-Bursevī, and al-Ālūsī mention creating means and removing obstacles, and al-Ālūsī adds patience under trials and dependence on God. Ibn ʿĀshūr names steadiness, courage, eloquence, and persuasive proof; al-Iṣlāḥī asks for a conducive route; Abū Ḥayyān notes Pharaoh's tyranny and the hardships of divine vicegerency. Al-Suyūṭī says the mission's coming hardship makes the plea apt. Al-Qurṭubī links heart, task, and tongue as aids in conveying. Asad states the request generally."}, {"id": "20:26/q06/p2", "position": "The difficult mission remains intact, but God makes it manageable for Moses himself.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī stresses that Moses did not seek a smaller mission or relaxation of its demands; lī marks personal facilitation."}, {"id": "20:26/q06/p3", "position": "All prophetic duties toward God and people, including revelation, worship, and preaching.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports a link to the whole divine address from 'I am your Lord': subtle knowledge, revelation, full worship, and preaching's hardships. Another account adds duties in the upper and lower worlds, whose demands can impede each other. Al-Ālūsī himself says the Pharaoh command implies all duties and the petition seeks help to fulfill them perfectly, without restricting the prayer to the earlier address."}, {"id": "20:26/q06/p4", "position": "Securing acceptance of God's religion among the mission's audience and support against opponents.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī interprets ease through the intended audience's receptivity and aid against resistance."}, {"id": "20:26/q06/p5", "position": "Actual execution and attainment of the mission's goal, beyond inward readiness.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports this reading as distinguishing the request for an open breast from the achieved result of the mission."}, {"id": "20:26/q06/p6", "position": "The ability to bear hearing other people's speech after hearing God's speech.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī places the eased affair alongside expansion of the breast and the burden of returning from divine speech to human speech."}]}
{"id": "20:26/q07", "question": "How does God bring about the requested ease?", "turns_on": "Whether facilitating action is described as God's creation of ease and will, as grace activating motives, or as grace made fitting by the request.", "positions": [{"id": "20:26/q07/p1", "position": "God creates ease and the servant's effective will.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports the Sunnī explanation. He argues no act happens without the servant's will; if the servant created that will, another will would be needed without end, so God creates it. He also reads breast expansion as recipient readiness and eased affair as effective agency, both granted by God's decree, wisdom, and power."}, {"id": "20:26/q07/p2", "position": "God supplies motives and incentives through facilitative acts of grace.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports this as the Muʿtazilite account."}, {"id": "20:26/q07/p3", "position": "The request can make further divine graces fitting at that time.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says God has already given every grace that could properly have been given, while some graces become fitting only after Moses asks."}]}
{"id": "20:26/q08", "question": "How does the eased affair fit with the other requests?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:26/q08/p1", "position": "It follows inner expansion and precedes effective speech in a sequence from readiness to conveying the mission.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says breast expansion gives spiritual light, ease helps acquire it, and the loosened tongue conveys it; the soul receives unseen forms through thought and teaches through speech. Al-Nasafī and al-Biqāʿī say the eased affair clarifies or reinforces the general request for an expanded breast. {"id": "20:26/q15", "question": "What relation between divine perfection and creating others does al-Rāzī discuss here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:26/q15/p1", "position": "God is eternally perfect in Himself and perfects others in time without any eternal defect.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī resumes his discussion of supplication under 2:286. {"id": "20:26/q16", "question": "Why does God bring some possibilities into existence and not all?", "turns_on": "Whether selective creation implies arbitrary withholding when human standards are applied to God's acts.", "positions": [{"id": "20:26/q16/p1", "position": "Creating all possibilities is impossible and would remove the distinction between capable agency and natural necessity.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says possible nonexistents are infinite, so creating all would put an infinity into existence; if all were created, no later creation could occur, seemingly turning capacity into incapacity. {"id": "20:26/q17", "question": "How does al-Rāzī describe mercy's successive gifts?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:26/q17/p1", "position": "Mercy grants existence, then life, then power, then reason and guidance to selected recipients.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says animals exceed inanimates through awareness and tool use; life to inanimacy is like light to darkness and existence to nonexistence. Reason completes four gifts, granting insight and guidance; he calls the last gift best by analogy with the final Prophet and humans among bodily creatures. {"id": "20:26/q18", "question": "How are divine gifts matched with worship and mission in al-Rāzī's discussion?", "turns_on": "Whether the parallel stops at four gifts and acts of prayer or adds prophethood and its mission.", "positions": [{"id": "20:26/q18/p1", "position": "Four gifts correspond to four services of prayer.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports an interpretation pairing existence, life, power, and reason with standing, recitation, bowing, and prostration, citing 20:14."}, {"id": "20:26/q18/p2", "position": "Prophethood is a fifth gift, matched by service in the prophetic mission.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports this further reading; Moses asks for help because his means are limited, his opponent powerful, and he is weak before the task."}]}
{"id": "20:26/q19", "question": "What other Qur'anic questions does al-Rāzī bring into this discussion?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:26/q19/p1", "position": "He points to question-and-answer passages on doctrine and law.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī lists the crescents, spirit, mountains, and Hour at 2:189, 17:85, 20:105, and 79:42; he also counts six successive legal questions in al-Baqara, starting with spending for parents and relatives at 2:215."}]}
{"id": "20:26/q20", "question": "What do the attached notes say about strange desert perceptions and unseen beings?", "turns_on": "How to weigh perceptual distortion against scriptural and transmitted testimony about unseen beings.", "positions": [{"id": "20:26/q20/p1", "position": "Some apparent forms and sounds may be distortions of ordinary perceptions.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba cites unattributed verses about a night echo and indistinct humanlike speech; al-Akhṭal's fox seeming an armored horse; al-Nābigha's elevated herder seeming a bird; and Ibn Aḥmar's multiplied shapes and pecking chameleon. {"id": "20:26/q21", "question": "How do the attached notes explain the Qur'an's seven letters and their tribal language?", "turns_on": "Which dialects supply the seven expressions, especially whether distinctively Yemeni forms are included.", "positions": [{"id": "20:26/q21/p1", "position": "The seven letters are forms drawn from seven Arabian tribal dialects, chiefly the relatively unaltered central dialects.", "reasons": "Al-Qāḍī permits transmitted differing forms. Abū ʿUbayd and others explain the letters as seven tribal languages, each contributing part. Ibn ʿAṭiyya begins with Quraysh and Banū Saʿd, then nearby Meccan tribes; his fuller list includes Kināna, Hudhayl, Thaqīf, Khuzāʿa, Asad, Ḍabba and associates, Tamīm, Qays, and related groups. Thābit ibn Qāsim gives a seven-group list: Quraysh, Kināna, Asad, Hudhayl, Tamīm, Ḍabba and associates, Qays. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says their eloquence and freedom from foreign influence made inimitability evident; central Ḥijāz, Najd, and Tihāma had less foreign contact. He says Iraq's neighboring languages, northern Syria, and later Mecca, Medina, and Ṭāʾif were affected by outsiders; later Basran and Kufan philologists preferred intermediate tribes, though the cities were purer in the Prophet's time. Seven tribal expressions may render one meaning with different eloquence and concision; Ibn ʿAbbās learned the meaning of faṭara from a Bedouin's claim to originate a well."}, {"id": "20:26/q21/p2", "position": "Distinctively Yemeni language is excluded, except words adopted by Ḥijāz Arabs.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya disputes the broader Yemeni inclusion attributed to Abū ʿUbayd and al-Mubarrad; he says distinctive expressions such as al-zakhīkh and al-qalūbī do not occur in the Qur'an."}]}

{"id": "20:42/q13", "question": "What is meant by My remembrance here?", "turns_on": "Whether remembrance denotes their own sustained recollection and worship, the public mission and its message, or particular subjects of that message.", "positions": [{"id": "20:42/q13/p1", "position": "Continual remembrance of God by heart and tongue, including praise, glorification and awareness of Him wherever they go.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī links it to God's blessings; al-Farrāʾ equates fī and min and calls for gratitude for divine kindness.
